gloss: To harm something so that it works less well or looks worse.
examples: Heavy rain *damaged* the roof over the porch.
Smoking *damages* your lungs a little at a time.
Two of the paintings were badly *damaged* in the fire.

gloss: To damage something so completely that it no longer exists or cannot be repaired.
examples: The fire *destroyed* three houses on our street.
One night of frost can *destroy* an entire crop.
The old bridge had been *destroyed* long before we got there.
contrast: The y after a vowel never changes: *destroyed*, *destroying* — not "destroied".

gloss: To spoil something completely so that it is no longer good or usable.
examples: The rain *ruined* my new suede shoes.
One careless word can *ruin* a friendship.
He was *ruining* the soup with all that salt.

gloss: To destroy something, especially a vehicle or a plan, through force or carelessness.
examples: He *wrecked* his father's car on the highway.
Don't let one bad review *wreck* your whole week.
The ship was *wrecked* off the coast of Maine.
contrast: The w is silent: *wreck* sounds like "reck", and the past *wrecked* is one syllable, ˈrɛkt.

gloss: To pull a building or structure down completely.
examples: The city plans to *demolish* the old cannery.
They *demolished* the stadium in a single morning.
The whole block is being *demolished* this spring.
contrast: Ends in -sh, so the third person adds -es: *demolishes*.

gloss: To destroy a place completely, or to shock and upset someone deeply.
examples: The hurricane *devastated* every town on the coast.
A late freeze can *devastate* the orange crop.
She was *devastated* by the news about her brother.

transitivity: both — transitive (*shatter* a window), intransitive (the glass *shattered*)
gloss: To break suddenly into many small pieces, or to break something that way.
examples: The mirror *shattered* when it hit the tile.
A stone off a truck can *shatter* a windshield.
There was *shattered* glass all over the sidewalk.

transitivity: both — transitive (*smash* a plate), intransitive (the car *smashed* into a wall)
gloss: To break something violently into pieces, or to hit something with great force.
examples: He *smashed* the window with a brick.
Careful — you'll *smash* the eggs under those cans.
The truck had *smashed* straight through the guardrail.

gloss: To press something so hard that it breaks or loses its shape.
examples: A falling branch *crushed* the garden shed.
Don't *crush* the strawberries at the bottom of the bag.
His hand was *crushed* in the press and never healed right.

transitivity: both — transitive (*crack* a nut), intransitive (the plate *cracked*)
gloss: To break so that a line appears on the surface, without breaking into pieces.
examples: The windshield *cracked* in the cold.
Set it down gently or you'll *crack* the tile.
She found a *cracked* pipe under the sink.

transitivity: both — transitive (*chip* a cup), intransitive (the paint *chipped*)
gloss: To break a small piece off the edge or surface of something hard.
examples: I *chipped* a tooth on a popcorn kernel.
The paint is *chipping* off the railing.
Every plate in the set is *chipped*.
contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the p doubles: *chipped*, *chipping*.

gloss: To make a thin mark or shallow cut on a surface with something sharp.
examples: The cat *scratched* the leather couch.
Don't *scratch* the screen with your keys.
The table was badly *scratched* by the movers.
contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: *scratches*.

gloss: To press or hit a surface so that it curves inward and leaves a hollow mark.
examples: A shopping cart *dented* my car door.
Aluminum this thin *dents* if you look at it.
The hood was *dented* in three places.

gloss: To damage a surface by rubbing it against something rough or sharp.
examples: He *scraped* the side of the van on a concrete post.
I fell off the bike and *scraped* my knee.
She spent an hour *scraping* old paint off the door.
contrast: Drop the silent e before -ing: *scraping*, not "scrapeing".

gloss: To mark or roughen a smooth surface, especially shoes or a floor, by rubbing.
examples: New shoes *scuff* fast on concrete.
He *scuffed* the hardwood dragging the couch across it.
Her boots were badly *scuffed* at the toe.

gloss: To tear something quickly and roughly.
examples: I *ripped* my jeans on a nail.
Please don't *rip* the envelope — I need the address.
The flag had been *ripped* to shreds by the wind.
contrast: The p doubles: *ripped*, *ripping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*snap* a stick), intransitive (the cable *snapped*)
gloss: To break suddenly with a sharp sound, usually into two pieces.
examples: The rope *snapped* under the weight.
Dry branches *snap* the moment you bend them.
He had *snapped* the pencil in half without noticing.
contrast: The p doubles: *snapped*, *snapping*.

gloss: To press something flat so that it loses its shape.
examples: Someone *squashed* the cake in my bag.
Don't *squash* the bread under the cans.
The berries were *squashed* at the bottom of the box.

gloss: To crush something into folds and wrinkles, or to fold up that way.
examples: He *crumpled* the letter and threw it in the trash.
Thin aluminum *crumples* if you so much as lean on it.
She smoothed out the *crumpled* receipt.

gloss: To break into thin, sharp pieces of wood or bone.
examples: The old door *splintered* when they forced it open.
Cheap plywood *splinters* as soon as you drill it.
He pulled a *splintered* board off the porch.

gloss: To break slowly into small pieces because something is old, dry, or weak.
examples: The brick wall is *crumbling* at the corner.
The cookie *crumbled* in my hand.
Years of rain had *crumbled* the stone steps.

transitivity: both — transitive (*collapse* the tent), intransitive (the roof *collapsed*)
gloss: To fall down suddenly because the structure gives way.
examples: The roof *collapsed* under the weight of the snow.
Old mine tunnels can *collapse* without any warning.
Two walls had already *collapsed* by the time the crew arrived.

gloss: To fall over, or to push something over, because it loses its balance.
examples: The wind *toppled* the fence along the driveway.
Stack them any higher and they'll *topple*.
A *toppled* streetlight was blocking both lanes.

gloss: To make something flat, or to knock it down level with the ground.
examples: The storm *flattened* the corn in a single night.
Heavy trucks *flatten* the gravel over time.
Whole villages were *flattened* by the earthquake.

gloss: To bend or twist out of shape, usually because of heat or moisture.
examples: Damp under the floor *warped* the boards.
Leave that vinyl in the sun and it will *warp*.
The back door is *warped* and won't close all the way.

gloss: To turn something out of its normal shape, or to injure a joint by turning it.
examples: He *twisted* his ankle on the bottom step.
Don't *twist* the cable like that — you'll break the wires inside.
The whole frame had been *twisted* in the crash.

gloss: To make a small hole in something so that air or liquid escapes.
examples: A nail *punctured* the rear tire.
Sharp rocks can *puncture* an inflatable raft.
He was treated for a *punctured* lung.

gloss: To make a hole through something with a sharp point.
examples: The nail *pierced* the sole of his boot.
She had her ears *pierced* last week.
A cold wind *pierces* right through this jacket.

gloss: To cut something with a long, violent stroke.
examples: Someone *slashed* the tires overnight.
He was *slashing* at the vines with a machete.
The seat had been *slashed* open with a knife.

gloss: To push a knife or other sharp point into someone or something.
examples: He *stabbed* the lid with a screwdriver to open it.
The victim had been *stabbed* twice in the arm.
Stop *stabbing* at the meat and use the knife properly.
contrast: The b doubles: *stabbed*, *stabbing*.

gloss: To cut something all the way through, separating it into parts.
examples: The blade *severed* the cable in one pass.
Ice storms often *sever* the power lines out here.
Surgeons reattached the *severed* finger.
contrast: Stress on the first syllable and no doubled r: *severed*, not "severred".

gloss: To burst apart with great force and noise.
examples: The gas tank *exploded* on impact.
Old fireworks can still *explode* years later.
A transformer had *exploded* two blocks away.

gloss: To break rock or a structure apart with explosives.
examples: Crews *blasted* a tunnel through the ridge.
They *blast* twice a day at the quarry.
The safe had been *blasted* open from behind.
contrast: The American vowel is æ: *blast* rhymes with *fast* — blæst, not blɑːst.

gloss: To attack a place with bombs.
examples: Planes *bombed* the rail bridge at dawn.
The city had been *bombed* for six straight weeks.
They kept *bombing* the same stretch of track.
contrast: The final b is silent: *bomb* is bɑːm, rhyming with *mom*.

gloss: To burn a surface slightly so that it darkens or changes color.
examples: I *scorched* my shirt with the iron.
The sun *scorches* the lawn every August.
There was a *scorched* ring on the countertop.

transitivity: both — transitive (*crash* the car), intransitive (the plane *crashed*)
gloss: To hit something violently while moving and be damaged, or to cause a vehicle to do this.
examples: She *crashed* the rental car on the first day.
Small planes *crash* more often than people think.
The truck had *crashed* through the guardrail and stopped in a ditch.

gloss: To hit something else while moving, usually with force.
examples: Two fishing boats *collided* in the fog.
The bus *collided* with a parked van.
Cars keep *colliding* at that intersection.
contrast: *collide* takes *with*: the truck *collided with* a wall.

gloss: To turn over onto its side or roof, or to tip something over.
examples: The tanker *overturned* on the exit ramp.
One big wave can *overturn* a boat that size.
An *overturned* trailer blocked the road for hours.

gloss: To die under water because you cannot breathe, or to kill something that way.
examples: Two swimmers nearly *drowned* off the pier.
Don't *drown* that plant — it needs very little water.
He was already *drowning* when the lifeguard reached him.

gloss: To cover a place with water, or to be covered with water.
examples: The river *flooded* the whole basement.
That underpass *floods* every spring.
We came home and found the kitchen *flooded*.
contrast: *flood* rhymes with *blood*: flʌd, not fluːd.

gloss: To damage public or private property on purpose.
examples: Somebody *vandalized* the bus shelter again.
Teenagers had *vandalized* every bench in the park.
They keep *vandalizing* the same stretch of wall.
contrast: American spelling -ize; British English writes *vandalise*.

gloss: To damage or spoil something deliberately so that it cannot work or succeed.
examples: Someone *sabotaged* the backup generator.
He *sabotages* his own interviews by showing up late.
The pipeline had been *sabotaged* twice that year.
contrast: French ending: the last syllable is ʒ, as in *measure*, not dʒ.

gloss: To spoil the surface or appearance of something, especially by writing or drawing on it.
examples: Vandals *defaced* the monument with spray paint.
It is a federal crime to *deface* currency.
Every sign on that road has been *defaced*.

gloss: To wreck something or make a complete mess of it.
examples: The band *trashed* the hotel room.
Don't let the dog *trash* the couch while we're out.
The kitchen was completely *trashed* after the party.
contrast: Informal American English; *trash* also means "throw away": I *trashed* the old receipts.

gloss: To damage a car so badly that repairing it would cost more than the car is worth.
examples: She *totaled* her truck on black ice.
One bad skid can *total* a brand-new car.
The insurance company declared it *totaled*.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *totaled*, *totaling*; British English writes *totalled*, *totalling*.

gloss: To weaken something gradually, often from below or from within.
examples: Water had *undermined* the foundation on the north side.
Constant criticism *undermines* a child's confidence.
He felt they were *undermining* him at every meeting.

gloss: To make something less strong, or to become less strong.
examples: Rust had *weakened* the beams under the deck.
Skipping meals *weakens* you faster than you'd think.
The storm is *weakening* as it moves inland.

gloss: To damage something so that it works less well than it should.
examples: Years on the factory floor *impaired* his hearing.
Even one drink can *impair* your driving.
Her vision is permanently *impaired*.

gloss: To break the normal course of an activity so that it cannot continue.
examples: The outage *disrupted* every flight out of Denver.
Protesters *disrupt* the hearing almost every week.
Service has been *disrupted* since Tuesday morning.

gloss: To take a machine or structure apart piece by piece.
examples: They *dismantled* the scaffolding in an afternoon.
You have to *dismantle* the bed to get it through the door.
The old refinery is being *dismantled* section by section.

gloss: To destroy something completely so that it never comes back.
examples: Smallpox was *eradicated* in 1980.
It takes years to *eradicate* termites from an old house.
Crews are still *eradicating* the last of the weeds along the creek.

gloss: To put an end to a law, system, or practice completely and officially.
examples: Congress *abolished* the tax in 1943.
Several states want to *abolish* the fee entirely.
The rule was *abolished* years before I started here.
contrast: Ends in -sh, so the third person adds -es: *abolishes*.

gloss: To injure someone, especially with a weapon.
examples: Two officers were *wounded* in the blast.
The shot *wounded* the animal but didn't kill it.
Careless words can *wound* worse than insults.
contrast: The verb *wound* wuːnd (to injure) is not the past of *wind*; that *wound* rhymes with *found*.

gloss: To hurt a person or animal so that part of the body is damaged.
examples: Six passengers were *injured* in the crash.
He *injured* his shoulder lifting boxes all afternoon.
Bad shoes will *injure* your knees over time.

gloss: To cause damage or injury to a person, an animal, or a thing.
examples: The runoff *harms* the fish downstream.
No one was *harmed* in the fire.
He never meant to *harm* anybody.

gloss: To injure skin or fruit so that a dark mark appears without the surface breaking.
examples: She *bruised* her elbow on the door frame.
Peaches *bruise* if you stack them three deep.
His arm was badly *bruised* from the fall.
contrast: Ends in a z sound: BROOZ, not "broos".

gloss: To injure a joint by twisting it suddenly.
examples: I *sprained* my wrist playing volleyball.
You can *sprain* an ankle just stepping off a curb.
He has been walking on a *sprained* knee for a week.

gloss: To crack or break a bone or a hard material.
examples: She *fractured* her wrist in the fall.
Freezing weather can *fracture* concrete.
The X-ray showed a *fractured* rib.

gloss: To harm or kill a living thing with a dangerous substance.
examples: Runoff from the mine *poisoned* the well.
Lead paint can *poison* small children.
Hundreds of fish were *poisoned* downstream.

gloss: To pass a disease to a living thing, or to fill something with harmful organisms.
examples: The cut got *infected* within a day.
One sick bird can *infect* the whole flock.
The virus had *infected* thousands before anyone noticed.

gloss: To make something dirty or dangerous by adding a harmful substance.
examples: Diesel from the tank *contaminated* the groundwater.
One dirty knife can *contaminate* the whole batch.
The soil is still *contaminated* thirty years later.

gloss: To make air, water, or land dirty and unsafe with waste or chemicals.
examples: The mill *polluted* the river for forty years.
Old engines *pollute* far more than new ones.
They were swimming in a heavily *polluted* lake.

gloss: To leave a colored mark on something that is hard to remove.
examples: Red wine *stained* the carpet by the door.
Coffee *stains* your teeth over the years.
He came out wearing a *stained* apron.

gloss: To spread something soft or wet over a surface, leaving dirty marks.
examples: The kids *smeared* jam all over the window.
Don't *smear* the ink — it's still wet.
Every mirror in the house was *smeared* with fingerprints.

gloss: To fix something broken or damaged so that it works again.
examples: A neighbor *repaired* the fence for us.
That little shop still *repairs* watches.
The bridge is being *repaired* all summer.

gloss: To repair something, or to put a problem right.
examples: Can you *fix* the dishwasher, or should we call someone?
He *fixed* the leak with a strip of tape.
Nothing has been *fixed* since we complained in March.
contrast: Verbs ending in -x add -es in the third person: *fixes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*mend* a shirt), intransitive (the bone *mended*)
gloss: To repair something small, especially clothing, or to heal.
examples: She *mended* the tear in his jacket.
Broken bones *mend* slowly at his age.
He spent the whole evening *mending* nets.

gloss: To cover a hole or a weak spot with a piece of material.
examples: He *patched* the inner tube and rode home.
The county *patches* the same stretch of road every spring.
The roof has been *patched* twice this year already.
contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: *patches*.

gloss: To bring something back to its original condition.
examples: They *restored* the theater to the way it looked in 1926.
Power was *restored* after eleven hours.
He spends every weekend *restoring* an old pickup.

gloss: To repair and improve an old building so that it is in good condition again.
examples: They *renovated* the entire second floor themselves.
We plan to *renovate* the kitchen next year.
The hotel is being *renovated* one floor at a time.

gloss: To change the structure or layout of a room or building.
examples: They *remodeled* the bathroom over two weekends.
We're *remodeling* the basement this fall.
A newly *remodeled* kitchen adds a lot to the price.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *remodeled*, *remodeling*; British English writes *remodelled*.

gloss: To clean and repair something old so that it looks and works like new.
examples: The company *refurbishes* returned laptops and resells them.
They *refurbished* the lobby over the winter.
I bought a *refurbished* phone for half the price.

gloss: To put a new thing in the place of one that is broken, worn out, or gone.
examples: We *replaced* the cracked tile by the door.
You should *replace* that smoke-detector battery every year.
All the windows have been *replaced* since we bought the place.
contrast: *replace* X *with* Y: they *replaced* the old pipe *with* copper.

gloss: To make something new, fresh, or valid again.
examples: I *renewed* my passport in March.
A week of rain *renews* the grass after a dry month.
His license has been *renewed* for another three years.
contrast: In American English *renew* is rɪˈnuː (ri-NOO), not "ri-NYOO".

gloss: To bring something back to life, to strength, or into use again.
examples: Paramedics *revived* him at the scene.
A little water will *revive* those plants.
The festival was *revived* after twenty years.

gloss: To check and repair a machine or vehicle as routine maintenance.
examples: I had the car *serviced* before the trip.
They *service* the elevators twice a year.
The furnace hasn't been *serviced* since we moved in.

gloss: To keep something in good condition by checking and repairing it regularly.
examples: The city *maintains* the bike paths along the river.
He *maintained* that old tractor for thirty years.
A well-*maintained* roof will last decades.

gloss: To make a small change to something so that it fits or works better.
examples: He *adjusted* the brakes in about five minutes.
You can *adjust* the strap right here.
The mirror had been *adjusted* for somebody much taller.

gloss: To make something firmer or less loose.
examples: *Tighten* the bolts before you ride it.
He *tightened* the loose hinge with a screwdriver.
Every screw on the shelf needed *tightening*.

gloss: To make something less tight or firm, or to become less tight.
examples: *Loosen* the nut a quarter turn, no more.
Vibration had *loosened* every screw in the panel.
The bolt is *loosening* on its own again.
contrast: The s here is an s sound, not z: LOO-suhn. Compare the adjective *loose* luːs with the verb *lose* luːz.

gloss: To join pieces of metal by heating them until they melt together.
examples: He *welded* a new bracket onto the frame.
They *weld* every seam by hand in that shop.
The crack had been *welded* shut years ago.

gloss: To join metal parts or wires with a melted metal alloy.
examples: She *soldered* the loose wire back onto the board.
You *solder* the joint, then let it cool completely.
The connection had been badly *soldered* at the factory.
contrast: In American English the l is silent: *solder* is SAH-dur, ˈsɑːdər.

gloss: To stick things together with glue.
examples: *Glue* the two halves and clamp them overnight.
He *glued* the broken handle back on.
She was *gluing* the pieces together when the phone rang.
contrast: The -ing form drops the e: *gluing*, not "glueing".

gloss: To fasten or repair something with sticky tape.
examples: He *taped* the cracked window until the new glass came.
I *tape* the boxes shut before stacking them.
The broken frame was *taped* together with duct tape.

gloss: To sew something with needle and thread, especially to close a tear or a wound.
examples: The doctor *stitched* the cut on his forehead.
She was *stitching* the strap back onto the bag when I came in.
That seam has been *stitched* twice already.

gloss: To close a gap or an opening so that nothing can get in or out.
examples: We *sealed* the cracks around the window before winter.
This caulk *seals* the joint around the tub.
The leak was *sealed* with a two-part epoxy.

gloss: To fill a hole so that nothing can pass or leak through it.
examples: He *plugged* the hole with a wooden peg.
A little putty will *plug* that gap for now.
The drain was *plugged* solid with hair.
contrast: The g doubles: *plugged*, *plugging*.

gloss: To rub a surface until it is smooth and shiny.
examples: He *polished* the scratched table until the marks disappeared.
She *polishes* her boots every Sunday night.
The floors had just been *polished* when we walked in.
contrast: The verb *polish* has a short o, ˈpɑːlɪʃ; the nationality *Polish* is ˈpoʊlɪʃ.

transitivity: both — transitive (*heal* a wound), intransitive (the cut *healed*)
gloss: To become healthy again after an injury, or to make someone healthy again.
examples: The burn *healed* in about two weeks.
Deep cuts *heal* slowly at his age.
His ankle still hasn't *healed* properly.
contrast: *heal* sounds exactly like *heel* — both hiːl.

gloss: To make an illness go away completely.
examples: Antibiotics *cured* the infection in three days.
Nothing *cures* a cold — you just wait it out.
She was *cured* after the second round of treatment.
contrast: *cure* removes the illness; *heal* closes the wound.

gloss: To wrap cloth around an injured part of the body.
examples: A nurse *bandaged* his hand at the clinic.
*Bandage* it firmly, but not so tight that it hurts.
His knee was still *bandaged* a month later.

gloss: To save something usable from a wreck, a fire, or a failing situation.
examples: They *salvaged* two engines from the wreck.
We *salvaged* what we could after the flood.
He is still trying to *salvage* the deal.

gloss: To build something again after it has been damaged or destroyed.
examples: The town *reconstructed* the bridge stone by stone.
Surgeons can *reconstruct* a knee like that in one operation.
The church is being *reconstructed* from old photographs.

gloss: To make a structure stronger by adding material or support.
examples: They *reinforced* the floor with steel beams.
We need to *reinforce* that shelf before we load it.
The wall is *reinforced* with concrete and rebar.

gloss: To make something stronger, or to become stronger.
examples: New bolts *strengthened* the joint considerably.
These exercises *strengthen* the muscles around the knee.
The dam has been *strengthened* twice since the flood.

gloss: To make something steady so that it stops moving, falling, or getting worse.
examples: Crews *stabilized* the leaning wall with steel cables.
His condition *stabilized* overnight.
They are *stabilizing* the slope above the road.
contrast: American spelling -ize; British English writes *stabilise*.

gloss: To keep something in good condition so that it is not damaged or lost.
examples: Cold, dry air *preserved* the documents for centuries.
The trust *preserves* historic barns across the county.
The ship's hull was perfectly *preserved* in the mud.

gloss: To become gradually worse in condition or quality.
examples: The road *deteriorated* badly after two hard winters.
Untreated wood *deteriorates* fast outdoors.
His health has been *deteriorating* since the spring.

gloss: To break down or lose quality over time, or to cause that to happen.
examples: Sunlight *degrades* cheap plastic in a single season.
The signal *degraded* the farther we drove.
All the rubber seals had *degraded* into powder.

gloss: To become worse, or to make something worse.
examples: The leak *worsened* overnight.
Road salt *worsens* the rust under the car.
Conditions on the mountain are *worsening* by the hour.

gloss: To be destroyed slowly by rotting or by natural breaking down.
examples: The fence posts *decayed* right at the ground line.
Teeth *decay* faster when you skip the dentist for years.
They pulled out the *decaying* floorboards.
contrast: The y stays after a vowel: *decayed*, *decaying* — compare *carry → carried*.

gloss: To wear something away slowly, especially by water or wind.
examples: The river *eroded* the bank right under the bridge.
Spring wind *erodes* the topsoil every year.
The cliff has been badly *eroded* since the last survey.

gloss: To destroy metal slowly by chemical action.
examples: Salt water *corroded* the bolts on the trailer.
Battery acid *corrodes* the contacts in a month.
The pipe was so *corroded* it crumbled in his hand.

transitivity: both — transitive (salt *rusts* the frame), intransitive (the gate *rusted*)
gloss: To become covered with the reddish-brown coating that forms on wet iron.
examples: The gate *rusted* through in five years.
Cheap tools *rust* if you leave them out overnight.
He finally replaced the *rusted* muffler.

gloss: To lose shine and turn dull and dark, the way silver does.
examples: The silverware *tarnished* in that damp drawer.
Brass *tarnishes* quickly near the ocean.
The scandal had *tarnished* his name for good.

gloss: To become worn at the edges so that threads or wires come loose.
examples: The cuffs *frayed* after one winter.
Cheap cable *frays* right where it bends.
He taped the *frayed* end of the cord.

gloss: To lose color, strength, or brightness little by little.
examples: The curtains *faded* in the afternoon sun.
Black shirts *fade* faster than white ones.
He was wearing a pair of *faded* jeans.

gloss: To dry up and shrink, the way a plant does without water.
examples: The tomatoes *withered* in the July heat.
Without rain the whole field *withers* by August.
She cut off the *withered* leaves.

gloss: To become limp and droop, especially of plants or greens.
examples: The lettuce *wilted* in the hot car.
Cut flowers *wilt* in a day without water.
He served us a plate of *wilted* spinach.

gloss: To break down completely in a liquid, or to make something do that.
examples: The tablet *dissolved* in warm water.
Salt *dissolves* faster if you stir it.
The sugar had *dissolved* into the syrup.
contrast: The double s is pronounced as z: di-ZAHLV, not "di-SOLV".

gloss: To use something up completely, or to tire someone out completely.
examples: The mine *exhausted* its best seam years ago.
Two night shifts in a row *exhaust* anybody.
We had *exhausted* every option by Friday.
contrast: The x here sounds like ɡz: ig-ZAWST, not "ek-SAWST".

gloss: To empty liquid out of something, or to use up strength or money.
examples: He *drained* the radiator before the first freeze.
The tank *drains* in about ten minutes.
The long repair had *drained* their savings.

gloss: To let liquid or gas escape through a hole or crack.
examples: The roof *leaked* all through April.
That valve *leaks* whenever it gets cold.
Oil was *leaking* onto the driveway all night.
contrast: *leak* sounds exactly like the vegetable *leek*.

transitivity: both — transitive (sand *jams* the lock), intransitive (the printer *jammed*)
gloss: To stick so that something cannot move or work, or to make it stick.
examples: The printer *jammed* twice this morning.
Fine sand *jams* the mechanism in a week.
That window has been *jammed* shut for years.
contrast: The m doubles: *jammed*, *jamming*.

gloss: To block a pipe or an opening so that nothing can pass through.
examples: Grease *clogged* the kitchen drain.
Leaves *clog* the gutters every fall.
The filter was completely *clogged* with dust.
contrast: The g doubles: *clogged*, *clogging*.

ru: выходить из строя, выйти из строя; отказывать, отказать
gloss: To stop working correctly.
examples: The alarm *malfunctioned* during the drill.
These sensors *malfunction* in freezing weather.
A *malfunctioning* pump flooded the whole basement.

ru: отказывать, отказать; выходить из строя; терпеть неудачу
gloss: To stop working, or to not succeed at something.
examples: The brakes *failed* halfway down the hill.
Hard drives *fail* without any warning.
The transmission had already *failed* twice that year.

transitivity: both — transitive (he *stalled* the car), intransitive (the engine *stalled*)
gloss: To stop running suddenly, the way an engine does.
examples: The car *stalled* at the light and wouldn't start.
It *stalls* every time I shift too early.
We were *stalling* out on the freeway with the flashers on.

gloss: To reach the end of the period during which something can be used.
examples: The warranty *expired* last month.
These batteries *expire* in 2029.
He was driving on an *expired* license.

gloss: To injure a muscle, or to pull something so hard that it is close to breaking.
examples: He *strained* his back moving the piano.
Don't *strain* that cable — it's already frayed.
The bolts were *strained* to the limit.

gloss: To grow old, or to change over time the way old things do.
examples: The rubber gaskets *aged* and finally cracked.
Cedar *ages* to a soft gray if you leave it bare.
The paint was *aging* badly on the south wall.
contrast: American English writes *aging* with one e; British English writes *ageing*.
